summary.text: The Roman Republic was the era of classical Roman civilisation from the overthrow of the Roman Kingdom, traditionally dated to 509 BC, until the Roman Empire was established in 27 BC.
During this period, Rome's control grew from the city's immediate surroundings to hegemony over the entire Mediterranean world.
Its government used annual magistracies overseen by a senate, but it was an elective oligarchy, with a number of powerful families largely monopolising the senior magistracies.

paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Roman Republic was the stretch of Roman history that began when the kings were overthrown, traditionally in 509 BC, and ended in 27 BC, when the Roman Empire was set up after the War of Actium. Over those centuries, Rome's reach grew from the land around the city to dominance over the whole Mediterranean world.

paragraphs.heading: The end of the kings
paragraphs.text: Before the Republic, Rome was ruled by kings, each chosen for life by the men of the Senate. Tradition says the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was driven out in 509 BC after his son Sextus raped a noblewoman named Lucretia. In that telling, a revolt led by the semi-mythical Lucius Junius Brutus ended the monarchy, and the king's powers passed to two consuls who served for one year, each able to block the other with a veto. Most modern scholars read these stories instead as a half-legendary version of an aristocratic coup inside Tarquin's own family, or of an Etruscan occupation, not a popular uprising.

paragraphs.heading: Elections, but few rulers
paragraphs.text: The Republic's form of government took shape at about the same time as direct democracy in ancient Greece. Its top public offices, the magistracies, were held jointly and for one year at a time, with a senate watching over them. Elections came every year, yet the system was not a true democracy but an elective oligarchy: a number of powerful families held most of the senior posts. In the early Republic these were the patricians, roughly 50 big families, known as gentes, who formed a closed circle and whose power came from their wealth, their land and their many clients.

paragraphs.heading: Patricians and plebs
paragraphs.text: Most citizens were commoners: small farmers, managers, craftsmen, traders and tenants who kept the economy running and could be called up in wartime. Few of them had much direct say in politics. In the early Republic the plebs, or plebeians, organised themselves as a separate group with their own internal ranks, laws and customs, yet they were barred from high religious and civil office. The poorest could refuse their labour in a walkout called a secessio plebis; the first, in 494 BC, protested the harsh treatment of plebeian debtors by the rich during a famine. This struggle, the Conflict of the Orders, ended peacefully, with the plebs winning political equality by the 4th century BC.

paragraphs.heading: A state almost always at war
paragraphs.text: Unlike the Empire in the era of the Pax Romana, the republican state was at war nearly all the time. Its first enemies were its Latin and Etruscan neighbours and the Gauls, who sacked Rome around 387 BC. Within a century of that sack, Rome had conquered most of the Italian peninsula and become one of the great powers of the Mediterranean. Its greatest rival was Carthage, which it fought three times. After winning at Zama in 202 BC, Rome became the leading Mediterranean power and went on to defeat rulers from Macedon to Egypt's queen Cleopatra.

paragraphs.heading: Strife at home
paragraphs.text: From 133 BC the late Republic was torn by conflict at home. A war with its Italian allies over citizenship, called the Social War, spread the violence much wider, and mass slavery helped bring about three Servile Wars. Violence in politics, together with powerful generals acting partly on their own, led to civil wars: first between Marius and Sulla, then in 49 BC between Julius Caesar and Pompey. Caesar won and was made dictator for life, but he was assassinated in 44 BC.

paragraphs.heading: From Republic to Empire
paragraphs.text: Caesar's heir Octavian and Caesar's lieutenant Mark Antony beat the assassins in 42 BC, then turned on each other. Antony and his ally and lover Cleopatra lost to Octavian at Actium in 31 BC. In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus, a moment often taken as the end of the Republic and the start of the Roman Empire.
